label: Radiation dose equivalent on the Mars surface, per sol (GCR, average)
source: Hassler et al. 2014, Science — Curiosity RAD at Gale: 0.64 ± 0.12 mSv per Earth day dose equivalent (absorbed 0.210 ± 0.040 mGy/day); × 1.027 for a sol
note: Was 0.67 labelled per sol: 0.67 is the SwRI press-release figure per Earth day. Measured at Gale (Aug 2012–Jun 2013, near solar maximum). Jezero sits ~1.8 km higher (thinner air): an estimated ~5–10% more dose, not applied (within RAD's ±19%).

label: Radiation dose during the cruise to Mars
source: Zeitlin et al. 2013, Science — RAD inside MSL during cruise

label: Earth-to-Mars transit time
source: Assumption: the RAD team's standard 180-day cruise scenario (Zeitlin et al. 2013: 2 × 180 d × 1.84 mSv/d ≈ 0.66 Sv round trip)
note: Used only to estimate dose already received on arrival.

label: NASA career radiation limit (effective dose)
source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev C (2023), requirement [V1 4030]: career effective dose < 600 mSv, all ages and sexes

label: NASA short-term radiation limit
source: NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev C (2023), Table 4.8-1: blood-forming organs 250 mGy-Eq per 30 days
note: mGy-Eq is absorbed dose weighted for tissue effects; it is not the same unit as RAD's mSv dose equivalent, so the app does not add them.

label: Dose Curiosity measured during the May 2024 solar storm
source: NASA/JPL, 10 Jun 2024: an astronaut next to Curiosity on 20 May 2024 would have received 8,100 micrograys (≈ 30 chest X-rays)
note: Absorbed dose (8.1 mGy), not mSv. NASA does not state the time window; RAD team material suggests it may be the event's peak daily rate rather than a total (event total possibly ~1.7 mGy). The app uses NASA's figure as reported.

label: Dose reduction from standing next to a butte
source: Ehresmann et al. 2021, Natural Radiation Shielding on Mars Measured With the MSL/RAD Instrument, JGR Planets 126(8), e2021JE006851
note: Paper abstract: Curiosity parked by Butte M12 (Murray Buttes), 19% of the sky blocked, sols 1456–1467: 4% lower dose rate, 7.5% fewer neutral particles. Value corrected from 5 to 4 to match the paper. One butte at Gale, not a general rule.

label: Days until most functional tasks recover after long spaceflight
source: Reschke, Kozlovskaya et al. 2015, joint NASA/Russian Pilot Field Test (NTRS 20150022287): clear improvement within 24 h, full recovery 6–16 days; functional tasks ~6 days (Miller et al. 2018)
note: Used for the walking-speed ramp. Full balance/agility can take up to ~2 weeks (obstacle course ~15 days, Mulavara et al. 2010); the app keeps a caution message until sol 16. Old citation (NTRS 20200001416) gave no recovery time.

label: Longest full sensorimotor recovery after long spaceflight (balance, agility)
source: Reschke, Kozlovskaya et al. 2015, Pilot Field Test (NTRS 20150022287): full recovery 6-16 days; obstacle course ~15 days (Mulavara et al. 2010)
note: Upper end of the measured range; used only for a caution message.

label: Walking speed on landing day vs normal
source: Team estimate based on post-flight sensorimotor findings
note: No study reports walking speed on landing day as a fraction of normal; obstacle-course times are much slower on day 1 (Mulavara 2010). Ramps linearly to 1.0 by sensorimotor_recovery_days; real recovery is faster at first.

label: Bone loss in weightlessness (1–1.5%/month)
source: NASA HRP Bone Fracture Evidence Report (Sibonga et al. 2017, NTRS 20170004597): 1–1.5%/month (pre-2009 average)
note: With the ISS resistance machine (ARED, from 2009) losses fell to ~0.3–0.5%/month (same report, Table 4). Never measured at Mars gravity.

label: Far-sighted vision shift from spaceflight (SANS), +0.5 to +1.75 D
source: Mader et al. 2011, Ophthalmology 118:2058 (NASA SANS evidence): shifts of +0.50 to +1.75 D

label: Distant-landmark range with SANS eye changes (no reduction)
source: No study links SANS to shorter distance vision: the far-sighted shift mainly blurs NEAR vision and is corrected with glasses (NASA SANS evidence; Mader et al. 2011)
note: Was 0.8 (team estimate with no basis). The SANS factor now warns about near vision (maps, displays) instead.

label: Design EVA duration
source: NASA suit design reference (NTRS 20170010189)
note: Plus ~2 h pre/post.

label: Consumables reserve kept back
source: Moore & Marmolejo 2014, Extravehicular Activity (EVA) Hardware & Operations Overview (NTRS 20140009556): EMU supports a 7 h EVA = 15 min egress + 6 h useful work + 15 min ingress + 30 min reserve
note: Shuttle/ISS EMU number, used here for a Mars suit.

label: Average metabolic rate during EVA
source: NASA suit design reference (NTRS 20170010189)
note: Shown as context; not used in maths v1.

label: Suited walk-back speed
source: Bellcomm memo B70 10028, P. Benjamin, 13 Oct 1970, 'Apollo 15 EVA Capability and Constraints Envelopes' (Case 320), p. 1 assumptions 7–8: planned walking traverses at 3.3 km/hr (1200 BTU/hr), emergency walkback at 3.3 km/hr (1440 BTU/hr); p. 2: walkback return to the LM at 3.3 km/hr
note: Lunar planning number used for Mars (0.38 g). ALSJ's Apollo 11 gaits page quotes 3.6 km/h (walks of about 1 h) and 2.7 km/h (longer). Measured Apollo 15 traverse speeds were 1.1–2.2 km/h; no suited walking speed has been measured at Mars gravity.

label: Safety margin on walk-home time (+20%)
source: Bellcomm memo B70 10028 (13 Oct 1970), p. 1 assumption 8: a 20% pad is required for emergency walkback (1200 → 1440 BTU/hr)
note: Apollo padded consumables (metabolic rate); the app applies the same 20% to walk-home time. Apollo used it so a crew could walk back if the rover failed.

label: Max slope allowed before sol 7
source: Team estimate
note: No NASA basis; a cautious team choice while balance recovers.

label: Max slope allowed after recovery
source: Team value, kept below NASA's Artemis III EVA planning limit of < 20° (NTRS 20240009596)
note: No Mars-specific suit slope limit exists. Apollo 15/16 traverses averaged ~5° with maxima ~22–25°.

label: Highest outside pressure NASA tested the suit water-membrane evaporator (SWME) against (~7 Torr)
source: NASA ICES-2024-463 (NTRS 20240005670): SWME tested at Mars back-pressure 5–7 Torr; sublimators 'cannot be used on the surface of Mars'
note: Replaces 'sublimator_max_pressure_pa': a sublimator needs pressure below water's triple point (611.657 Pa), and Jezero is ~625–761 Pa, so it cannot cool a suit there. Above the tested range the evaporator's margin is unknown. NASA's 2026 Mars PLSS study pairs the SWME with a vacuum pump.

label: Water's triple point: a suit sublimator only works below this outside pressure
source: Wagner & Pruß 2002 (IAPWS-95), J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 31:387
note: Physics constant. Jezero's pressure is above it, so space-station style sublimator cooling is ruled out on Mars.

label: Typical surface pressure at Jezero (~5.4 Torr)
source: Perseverance MEDA (Sánchez-Lavega et al. 2023, JGR Planets): daily means ~625 (Ls 101°) to ~761 Pa (Ls 55°)
note: Typical value; −13% / +6% seasonal range over Ls 13–241°, daily swing 20–50 Pa.

label: Mean air temperature at Jezero
source: Perseverance MEDA
note: Air −83 to −23 °C over a sol (MEDA team); day–night swing ~50–60 °C (Rodríguez-Manfredi et al. 2023).

label: Cold warning threshold
source: Team estimate

label: Be heading home by (cooling before dusk)
source: Team estimate
note: Team threshold; the near-surface air starts its evening cooling around 17 LTST (Munguira et al. 2023).

label: Dust-devil warning window start
source: Newman et al. 2022, Science Advances 8:eabn3783 (Perseverance MEDA): >4 vortices (pressure drops >0.5 Pa) per sol, over 25% of them dusty; peak 12–13 LTST
note: Window widened by 1 h each side.

label: Dust-devil warning window end
source: Newman et al. 2022

label: Peak dust-devil wind seen at Jezero
source: Newman et al. 2022
note: Maximum vortex wind seen, not typical. Largest dust devil imaged ~270 m wide (typical 25–29 m, Hueso et al. 2023); pressure drop up to ~6.5 Pa.

label: What a 32 m/s Mars wind pushes like on Earth
source: Team calculation: same dynamic pressure, Mars air density ≈ 1/80 of Earth
note: 32 × sqrt(ρMars/ρEarth). Midday air (~−20 °C, when dust devils occur): ρ ≈ 1/80 of Earth → 3.6 m/s; at the −55 °C mean ρ ≈ 1/70 → 3.8 m/s.

label: Normal dust optical depth at Jezero
source: Lemmon et al. 2022 (Perseverance)
note: Lemmon et al. 2022: ~0.3 before and ~0.4 after the Jan 2022 storm (Ls 150–160°); higher in the dusty season.

label: Dust optical depth in the Jan 2022 Jezero storm
source: Lemmon et al. 2022
note: Peak ~2 (1.7 on sols 313–315), up from ~0.3; both wind-sensor booms damaged; the storm affected Jezero for ~6 sols.

label: Dust caution threshold
source: Team estimate
note: Team heuristic: NASA has no numeric dust limit for EVA (NASA/TM-2018-220084).

label: Dust return threshold
source: Team estimate
note: Team heuristic: NASA has no numeric dust limit for EVA (NASA/TM-2018-220084).

label: Dust layer depth used to turn τ into visibility (well-mixed dust ≈ gas scale height)
source: Lemmon et al. 2022 (Perseverance) express line-of-sight dust opacity per 10.5 km (≈ the gas scale height); Koschmieder V = 3.912 / (τ / H)
note: Model. τ 2 → ~21 km, τ 10 → ~4 km. Check: in Jan 2022 a hill 36 km away was 'only faintly visible' at τ ≈ 1.3/10.5 km (model ~32 km). When dust settles low after a storm, visibility is worse: Curiosity measured 2.7 km at Gale (2018, column τ ~8; model ~5 km) — that case is what 'Lost in dust' mode is for. Was 15 km (no source).

label: Perchlorate in Martian soil (Phoenix: 0.4–0.6% by mass)
source: Hecht et al. 2009, Science 325:64 (Phoenix WCL): 0.4–0.6 wt% perchlorate; Curiosity at Gale 0.05–1.05 wt% (Sutter et al. 2017)
note: Thyroid risk → dust-off before entry. Was 0.75 ('0.5–1%', which mixed two sites).

label: How much longer a sol is than an Earth day
source: Sol = 24 h 39 min 35 s; circadian study (PMC1934931)
note: Mars24: sol = 88,775.244 s = 24 h 39 min 35.244 s → 39.587 min longer than an Earth day.

label: One Mars hour (1/24 sol) in Earth minutes
source: Sol length 88,775 s / 24

label: Astronaut eye height in suit
source: Team estimate

label: Position uncertainty growth without a fix (dead reckoning)
source: Team estimate within published ranges: Apollo LRV navigation requirement ±2% of distance; foot-mounted IMUs ~1–2% with zero-velocity updates, low-cost units 7–12%
note: Mars has no global magnetic field, so no compass: heading comes from a gyro re-set against the Sun or stars (as Apollo's LRV sun-shadow device). Uncertainty circle = last fix + 3% of distance walked since; reset by Horizon Match.

label: Smallest uncertainty a Horizon Match fix may claim
source: Nash et al. 2024, ICRA (JPL): horizon-matching localisation is typically on the order of 100 m, at best 10 m
note: The simulated test often says less (50 m); the app never shows a fix as better than published real-world accuracy.

label: How fast a dust devil drifts across the ground
source: Team estimate: dust devils travel with the background wind, typically a few m/s
note: Only used for the illustrative map animation.
